collaborations.artifact: The subject expert groups ordinary and exceptional cases by the work required. Finance calculates each group’s cost separately and marks effort that has not yet been measured. Fictional example: Illustrative ordinary review costs EUR 1; an exception takes EUR 8 specialist effort. Keep these categories separate in the pilot cost model.

collaborations.title: Keep approval tied to the exact draft
collaborations.question: How will an edited draft require approval again before it is submitted?
collaborations.artifact: The designer specifies the approval and edited-draft screens. The engineer records the exact fields and revision covered by approval, then rejects an attempt to reuse approval after a change. Fictional example: Customer approves draft r3 for item HH2 at address A; changing to address B creates r4 and requires new approval.

collaborations.title: Let keyboard users recover
collaborations.question: How can a keyboard user correct the product choice and return to the same question?
collaborations.artifact: The designer specifies the correction steps, retained text and next keyboard focus. The junior engineer implements that scenario and demonstrates it without using a mouse. Fictional example: After keyboard selection changes HH1 to HH2, return focus to the question and retain “How do I reset it?”.

collaborations.title: Show what happened after an interruption
collaborations.question: Can the user tell whether an interrupted request actually created an order?
collaborations.artifact: The designer writes distinct messages for drafts, submissions and uncertain completion. The test engineer checks them against stored order state so a lost reply does not invite an accidental second order. Fictional example: If order O-17 exists but acknowledgement was lost, show “Checking order O-17” rather than inviting a second order.

collaborations.title: Explain a service interruption
collaborations.question: What should users see and keep while maintenance prevents requests from being processed?
collaborations.artifact: The DevOps engineer names the interruption and what remains available. The designer writes the paused-service message and draft-recovery steps, then they check that the promised recovery is supported. Fictional example: During incompatible maintenance, show “Requests are paused; contact support”; preserve the draft locally.

collaborations.title: Show progress only after it happens
collaborations.question: What message accurately describes a request waiting for a person to review it?
collaborations.artifact: The reliability engineer identifies the recorded event that confirms a queue accepted the request. The designer maps that event to visible wording and keeps an unsent draft in a different state. Fictional example: Only show “Awaiting specialist review” after queue acknowledgement Q-17; an unsubmitted draft is “Not sent”.

collaborations.title: Include extra user and staff effort in cost
collaborations.question: Does a cheaper system create extra corrections, user steps or staff work?
collaborations.artifact: The designer identifies the added steps and likely recovery work. Finance includes that work in the comparison instead of comparing hosting charges alone. Fictional example: Illustrative form A costs 20 units less to host but sends 100 extra address corrections to staff at 1 unit each. Its complete cost is 80 units higher.

collaborations.title: Review a small change against its rule
collaborations.question: Which input proves that the change follows the intended rule at its limit?
collaborations.artifact: The junior engineer writes a test that fails before the change and passes after it. The technical lead reviews the rule, test and code together rather than accepting a passing test alone. Fictional example: For purchase P1, test amount=1001 and requesterRole=team-lead: route=Finance, exceptionApproved=false and submittedPurchases=0.

collaborations.title: Keep expected answers independent of the code
collaborations.question: Where does the expected answer come from, apart from the function being tested?
collaborations.artifact: The test engineer derives the expected result from the approved rule or source. The engineer runs the implementation against it; an oracle is this independently established expected result. Fictional example: Expected reset duration comes from HH2-r3 (10 seconds), not from the function’s returned value.

collaborations.title: Restore the same set of release parts
collaborations.question: Which software, source and settings versions must be deployed or restored together?
collaborations.artifact: The engineer identifies compatible parts. The DevOps engineer records them in a release manifest, a list of exact versions, and writes the restoration steps and checks. Fictional example: Restore app r6, prompt p2, source collection c3 and rules r1 together; repeat the check that denies access to another customer organisation’s private records.

collaborations.title: Recover when an action’s reply is lost
collaborations.question: How does the service find out whether an action succeeded without accidentally doing it twice?
collaborations.artifact: The engineer defines request identifiers and states for partial failure. The reliability engineer uses them to recover; idempotency means repeating the same request does not create another effect. Fictional example: Request K-17 created O-17 before timeout; retry K-17 returns O-17 and order count remains one.

collaborations.title: Compare the cost of designs that meet the need
collaborations.question: Which observed demand or quality problem justifies a larger model or another service?
collaborations.artifact: The engineer records quality and capacity results for each design. Finance includes their full cost and compares the extra cost with the agreed value of avoiding errors. Fictional example: Illustrative candidate saves 2 quality failures per 100 cases but doubles cost; retain the smaller model unless the agreed error-cost criterion justifies expansion.

collaborations.title: Prove that the test catches a defect
collaborations.question: Which deliberate test-only mistake should make this check fail, and for what reason?
collaborations.artifact: The junior engineer introduces a controlled defect in an isolated test run. The test engineer checks that the expected assertion fails and preserves the output; this is mutation testing. Restore the correct code afterward. Fictional example: Temporarily remove P1’s amount check. A 1200-unit team-lead request now submits a purchase; the expected no-submission assertion must fail.

collaborations.title: Make another person able to run the example
collaborations.question: Which unstated local setting or file does another contributor need to reproduce the result?
collaborations.artifact: The junior engineer follows the setup instructions from a clean environment. The DevOps engineer fixes missing setup steps and supplies a fixture, a fixed sample dataset, without sharing credentials. Fictional example: Use the documented source-data fixture c4 with simulated model calls; a developer’s unstated local search index cannot be required.

collaborations.title: Find the first wrong step in a request
collaborations.question: Which recorded step first differs from the expected path?
collaborations.artifact: The reliability engineer provides a trace, a record of the steps in a request, with fictional data. The junior engineer identifies the first wrong value and asks the relevant owner to investigate. Fictional example: Trace request R17: product=Business, retrievedSource=HH2-r3. Escalate the first incorrect retrieval scope, before answer generation.

collaborations.title: Calculate the cost of a request path
collaborations.question: Which repeat call or retry changes the cost of completing this user task?
collaborations.artifact: The junior engineer counts calls along the path and shows the units. Finance checks the price assumptions and divides total cost by completed successes rather than by all attempts. Fictional example: Illustrative 3 calls at EUR 0.01 each cost EUR 0.03 per request; 2 successful requests out of 3 give EUR 0.09/2 = EUR 0.045 per success.

collaborations.title: Match release evidence to the release
collaborations.question: How does the release process reject passing test results that belong to an older version?
collaborations.artifact: The test engineer records which exact release files were tested. The DevOps engineer checks their digest, a content fingerprint, against the candidate before permitting release; a mismatched record blocks it. Fictional example: Results for app r6 cannot satisfy app r7’s release gate; require an evidence record whose artifact digest matches r7.

collaborations.title: Retain an incident as a known-failure test
collaborations.question: Which incident should become a test without being counted as unseen evaluation data?
collaborations.artifact: The reliability engineer supplies the incident record with permitted data. The test engineer turns it into a regression test and keeps a separate holdout, a set not inspected during development, for final comparison. Fictional example: Incident I17 becomes regression R17; it does not enter untouched H01–H10 after the team has inspected it.

collaborations.title: Check quality before accepting a saving
collaborations.question: Does the cheaper design still meet the agreed task target, including difficult cases and uncertainty?
collaborations.artifact: The test engineer compares both designs on the same cases and reports important groups separately. Finance reviews those results before calling the cost saving acceptable. Fictional example: Cheaper B passes 88/100 vs A 90/100; inspect paired failures and uncertainty before declaring the cost saving acceptable.

collaborations.title: Practise restoring a working release
collaborations.question: Can the responder restore an earlier compatible release while preserving records and access restrictions?
collaborations.artifact: The DevOps engineer prepares the previous release and restoration steps. The reliability engineer rehearses them and records access and existing-record checks before the service is reopened. Fictional example: Restore r6/c3, deny customer organisation A access to organisation B’s ticket B-17, and confirm existing order O-17 remains queryable.

collaborations.title: Identify costs that continue without traffic
collaborations.question: Which charges remain payable if fewer requests arrive than planned?
collaborations.artifact: The DevOps engineer lists provisioned resources and their charges. Finance separates fixed costs, which remain without requests, from variable charges that depend on use. Fictional example: An illustrative EUR 100 monthly instance fee remains payable at zero requests; per-call charges fall with volume.

collaborations.title: Fund the support needed for the service target
collaborations.question: Does the agreed service target remain affordable when reviews, retries and incidents require more work?
collaborations.artifact: The reliability engineer records the work needed to meet the service target. Finance recalculates cost and asks the service owner to decide changes to the target, staffing or budget. Fictional example: Illustrative review load doubles from 100 to 200 cases at EUR 1 each; the service owner and finance revisit the EUR 500 cap.
